answer:
**Different anomaly detectors define “unusual” differently.** Isolation Forest asks how quickly random splits separate a point. An isolated extreme value can often be cut off with a short path, while a point in a dense group requires more splits. One-class SVM estimates a boundary around supported data. LOF compares a point's local density with its neighbors. An autoencoder treats large reconstruction error as suspicious. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

Consider a sparse small cluster beside a dense large cluster. A global density rule may call the entire small cluster anomalous, while a local comparison can recognize that its members resemble one another. Conversely, a powerful autoencoder might reconstruct some anomalies well, so low error does not prove normality.

**Complexity depends on the implementation.** Isolation Forest commonly builds T trees on subsamples of size psi. Its training cost is then roughly $O(T\psi\log\psi)$ under typical balanced behavior, while scoring N points costs about $O(NT\log\psi)$. Calling it universally O(N log N) hides those choices.

Select thresholds using operational capacity and known validation cases. Check high-dimensional noise, drift, and contamination. An anomaly score is a ranking of unusualness under a model, not automatically a calibrated fraud probability or evidence of wrongdoing. Compare detectors on the kinds of novelty the application actually needs to catch.

**Technical details and references.**

Isolation Forest scores points by average path length under random feature/threshold partitions: unusual points can often be isolated with fewer splits. One-class SVM learns a support boundary; LOF compares local density to neighbors; autoencoders use reconstruction error, which may also be low for some anomalies. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

Isolation Forest's cost is better stated using tree count $T$ and subsample size $\psi$: training is roughly $O(T\psi\log\psi)$ under typical balanced behavior, and scoring $O(NT\log\psi)$. It is not universally $O(N\log N)$ or guaranteed shallow for every anomaly.

Evaluate contamination assumptions, high-dimensional noise, and deployment novelty separately. Thresholds need operational calibration; an anomaly score is not automatically a fraud probability or a reason to take action.
